newsitem.title: USA: Paper shares rise with James River deal.
newsitem.headline: Paper shares rise with James River deal.

text.p: The shares of major U.S. paper and pulp producers rose Monday on speculation there would be more consolidation in the sector after the announcement of a $5.8 billion merger of Fort Howard Corp and the James River Corp.

Analysts said the sector, which has delivered disappointing earnings for several quarters, also got a boost from a Bear Stearns analyst's report on International Paper that said the stock was a potential turn around story.

Industry-leader International Paper was among the 25 most actively traded stocks on the New York Exchange. In afternoon trading, IP rose 2-1/8 to 45-1/4. Boise Cascade Corp rose 1-1/2 to 34-3/8 and Georgia-Pacific Corp was at 81-1/2, after closing Friday at at 78. Similarly, while Consolidated Papers was up 1-3/4 to 56-5/8 and Mead Corp was up 2-3/8 to 58-1/2.
Linda Lieberman, the Bear Stears analyst who upgraded IP to a buy from a neutral, said she raised the company's rating because "it's a potential turnaround story."
"The group is turning up as a whole for seasonal reasons and there are lots of price increases," she said, although she was, as are others, unwilling to say they will hold.
"People are getting excited about the companies. The market is at 7,000 and this is a group that hasn't moved. And we should see more consolidations."
Added UBS Securities analysts Mark Diverio: "The news of the proposed merger probably has people focused on the group and there is some bounce from that since the group has lagged the market.
"The second quarter could be the earnings trough for these companies. The stocks are relatively cheap and relatively safe at a time when the market is quite volatile."

The industry is also rife with rumours about who will buy whom next. Those mentioned include large ones like Boise Cascade Corp, as well as some of the industry's smaller players: Potlatch Corp, Chesapeake Corp and P.H. Glatfelter Co, for example. Representatives from these companies were not immediately available for comment.
Some who follow the industry believe that, although further mergers would be healthy, the industry overall is not financially healthy enough to support them.
Producers are trying to rein in production excesses, one of the prime reasons industry earnings have been bleak for the past few quarters.
"I think there is a trend we've been seeing which is rationalization," said UBS's Diverio.

"Companies have been divesting specific mills or divisions not part of their core operations to become more focused. We've been seeing a slew of these over the past four or five years and they don't get the headlines like big deals do."
